title: Reclaim lock screen keyboard focus after resume from suspend
author: jonathan-downs
body:
## Summary

- The lock screen's password field only regrabs keyboard focus when `inputEnabled` toggles or when the user clicks/moves the pointer on the lock surface (`LockView`'s `wakeRequested`). A real suspend/resume does neither: the lock was already active before the machine slept, so `inputEnabled` never changes, and there's no pointer activity on resume. The surface comes back with no focused input, so nothing you type registers until you click the screen.
- Adds `omarchy-resume-focus-monitor.service`, a systemd user service mirroring the existing `omarchy-sleep-lock.service`, running `bin/omarchy-system-resume-monitor`. It watches logind's `PrepareForSleep` signal for the resume case (`boolean false`) and calls a new `lock` IPC verb, `resume()`, on each occurrence.
- `lock/Service.qml`'s `resume()` IPC handler calls a new `handleSystemResume()` that reuses `runWake()` and bumps a new `resumeSignal` property, wired into `LockView` so it reclaims focus the same way the click handler already does.

**Note on design:** my first pass ran the monitor as a plain QML `Process` owned by `Service.qml` instead of a systemd service. Testing on real hardware caught a real leak in that approach: when Quickshell itself is torn down (a shell restart, a crash-and-relaunch), the `Process`'s own child can be killed abruptly enough that its coproc'd `dbus-monitor` grandchild is orphaned rather than reaped, reparenting to the user's systemd instance and leaking a live system-bus connection indefinitely. Reproduced across multiple shell restarts before fixing it. The systemd-service approach here avoids that entirely: the whole unit's cgroup (dbus-monitor included) is torn down together regardless of how the service itself exits, matching the existing pre-sleep monitor's own approach for the same reason.

## Related

Encountered while investigating a report involving a suspend/resume-specific numpad quirk on the lock screen (separate root cause, not addressed here). This PR only covers the confirmed, reproducible focus issue. It touches the same file as a few other open suspend/resume + lock-screen issues, so linking for context in case of overlapping work:

- #11820
- #12140
- #11744

## Test plan

- [x] `./test/cli` - all passing
- [x] `./test/shell` - all passing except 5 pre-existing failures unrelated to this change and reproducible on a clean checkout (`config-test.sh`, `locate-test.sh`, `omarchy-kernel-migration-test.sh`, `snapper-test.sh`, `unowned-system-paths-test.sh`)
- [x] New `test/shell.d/resume-monitor-test.sh`: verifies the monitor calls `omarchy-shell lock resume` once per resume event while ignoring sleep events, cleans up its `dbus-monitor` producer when the pipeline itself is killed directly (bypassing systemd, to prove the script doesn't rely on systemd alone), and that `--consume` parses events correctly from stdin. Ran 5x in a loop with no leaked processes.
- [x] New assertions in `test/shell.d/systemd-test.sh` for the service file's `ExecStart` path, environment/ordering conditions, `Restart=always`, and that first-run enables it
- [x] Verified locally on real hardware via a plugin clone of `lock` plus the real systemd service: lid-close suspend/resume no longer requires a click before the password field accepts input, and confirmed zero leaked `dbus-monitor` processes across multiple shell restarts and service (re)starts

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

@@ -0,0 +1,51 @@
+#!/bin/bash
+
+# omarchy:summary=Monitor system resume from suspend and nudge lock screen focus
+# omarchy:group=system
+# omarchy:hidden=true
+
+# Unlike omarchy-system-sleep-monitor, this has no inhibitor to hold and no
+# single event to wait for: it runs for as long as the service does and calls
+# into the shell on every resume. Run under a systemd service (see
+# default/systemd/user/omarchy-resume-focus-monitor.service) rather than as a
+# Quickshell Process, so a restart or crash cannot orphan the dbus-monitor
+# child -- systemd kills the whole unit's cgroup, where a plain child process
+# of the shell can outlive it if the shell itself is torn down abruptly. The
+# coproc/trap below is a second, independent line of defense so the script
+# doesn't rely on that alone: it reaps its own producer even when run outside
+# systemd (as in tests, or a manual invocation).
+consume_resume_events() {
+  local line
+
+  while IFS= read -r line; do
+    [[ $line == *"boolean false"* ]] && omarchy-shell lock resume >/dev/null 2>&1
+  done
+}
+
+monitor_resume_events() {
+  local monitor_fd monitor_pid
+
+  coproc RESUME_EVENTS {
+    exec dbus-monitor --system \
+      "type='signal',sender='org.freedesktop.login1',interface='org.freedesktop.login1.Manager',member='PrepareForSleep'"
+  }
+  monitor_fd=${RESUME_EVENTS[0]}
+  monitor_pid=$RESUME_EVENTS_PID
+
+  cleanup_monitor() {
+    kill "$monitor_pid" 2>/dev/null || true
+    wait "$monitor_pid" 2>/dev/null || true
+  }
+  trap cleanup_monitor EXIT
+
+  consume_resume_events <&"$monitor_fd"
+}
+
+case ${1:-} in
+  --consume)
+    consume_resume_events
+    exit 0
+    ;;
+esac
+
+monitor_resume_events

@@ -0,0 +1,20 @@
+[Unit]
+Description=Reclaim lock screen keyboard focus after resume from suspend
+# Same rationale as omarchy-sleep-lock.service: the monitor calls into the
+# running Omarchy shell, so wait until UWSM has imported OMARCHY_PATH and
+# WAYLAND_DISPLAY, but keep the default target ordering so the monitor starts
+# before graphical-session.target is reached.
+After=dbus.socket wayland-session-waitenv.service
+Requires=dbus.socket
+PartOf=graphical-session.target
+ConditionEnvironment=OMARCHY_PATH
+ConditionEnvironment=WAYLAND_DISPLAY
+
+[Service]
+Type=simple
+ExecStart=/usr/bin/omarchy-system-resume-monitor
+Restart=always
+RestartSec=2
+
+[Install]
+WantedBy=graphical-session.target

@@ -16,6 +16,7 @@ systemctl --user enable --now \
   bt-agent.service \
   omarchy-recover-internal-monitor.service \
   omarchy-sleep-lock.service \
+  omarchy-resume-focus-monitor.service \
   omarchy-migrate-notify.service \
   omarchy-fcitx5.service \
   omarchy-crash-watch.service

@@ -0,0 +1,111 @@
+#!/bin/bash
+
+set -euo pipefail
+
+source "$(cd -- "$(dirname -- "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)/base-test.sh"
+
+resume_monitor="$ROOT/bin/omarchy-system-resume-monitor"
+tmpdir=$(mktemp -d)
+trap 'rm -rf "$tmpdir"' EXIT
+
+mock_bin="$tmpdir/bin"
+producer_pid_file="$tmpdir/producer-pid"
+call_log="$tmpdir/calls"
+mkdir -p "$mock_bin"
+: >"$call_log"
+
+# Emits a sleep event, a resume event, then another sleep/resume pair, to
+# prove the monitor keeps running and calling into the shell on every resume
+# rather than exiting after the first one -- unlike the pre-sleep monitor,
+# this has no inhibitor lock tying it to a single event.
+cat >"$mock_bin/dbus-monitor" <<'SH'
+#!/bin/bash
+
+echo "$$" >"$PRODUCER_PID_FILE"
+printf '   boolean true\n'
+printf '   boolean false\n'
+printf '   boolean true\n'
+printf '   boolean false\n'
+exec sleep 30
+SH
+chmod +x "$mock_bin/dbus-monitor"
+
+cat >"$mock_bin/omarchy-shell" <<'SH'
+#!/bin/bash
+
+printf 'shell %s\n' "$*" >>"$CALL_LOG"
+SH
+chmod +x "$mock_bin/omarchy-shell"
+
+PATH="$mock_bin:$PATH" CALL_LOG="$call_log" PRODUCER_PID_FILE="$producer_pid_file" \
+  "$resume_monitor" &
+monitor_pid=$!
+sleep 0.5
+kill "$monitor_pid" 2>/dev/null || true
+wait "$monitor_pid" 2>/dev/null || true
+
+mapfile -t calls <"$call_log"
+
+[[ ${#calls[@]} -eq 2 && ${calls[0]} == "shell lock resume" && ${calls[1]} == "shell lock resume" ]] ||
+  fail "resume monitor calls into the shell once per resume, ignoring sleep events" \
+    "calls: ${calls[*]:-<none>}"
+pass "resume monitor calls into the shell once per resume, ignoring sleep events"
+
+# Terminating the monitor must also clean up the dbus-monitor producer instead
+# of orphaning it -- this is the leak the systemd unit (Restart=always plus
+# cgroup teardown) guards against; the script's own pipeline shouldn't leak
+# one either when killed directly.
+rm -f "$producer_pid_file"
+cat >"$mock_bin/dbus-monitor" <<'SH'
+#!/bin/bash
+
+sleep 0.1
+echo "$$" >"$PRODUCER_PID_FILE"
+exec sleep 30
+SH
+chmod +x "$mock_bin/dbus-monitor"
+
+PATH="$mock_bin:$PATH" CALL_LOG="$call_log" PRODUCER_PID_FILE="$producer_pid_file" \
+  "$resume_monitor" &
+monitor_pid=$!
+
+for _ in {1..100}; do
+  [[ -s $producer_pid_file ]] && break
+  sleep 0.01
+done
+if [[ ! -s $producer_pid_file ]]; then
+  kill "$monitor_pid" 2>/dev/null || true
+  wait "$monitor_pid" 2>/dev/null || true
+  fail "resume monitor starts its event producer"
+fi
+
+producer_pid=$(<"$producer_pid_file")
+kill "$monitor_pid"
+wait "$monitor_pid" 2>/dev/null || true
+
+# The producer is allowed a moment to receive and act on the pipeline's own
+# teardown before this counts as a leak.
+for _ in {1..20}; do
+  kill -0 "$producer_pid" 2>/dev/null || break
+  sleep 0.05
+done
+if kill -0 "$producer_pid" 2>/dev/null; then
+  kill "$producer_pid" 2>/dev/null || true
+  fail "resume monitor cleans up its producer when the pipeline itself is terminated" \
+    "producer still running: $producer_pid"
+fi
+pass "resume monitor cleans up its producer when the pipeline itself is terminated"
+
+# --consume reads events straight off stdin, the same seam the pre-sleep
+# monitor's tests use, so the parsing logic is testable without a real (or
+# even mocked) dbus-monitor process.
+rm -f "$call_log"
+: >"$call_log"
+printf '   boolean true\n   boolean false\n   garbage\n   boolean false\n' \
+  | PATH="$mock_bin:$PATH" CALL_LOG="$call_log" "$resume_monitor" --consume
+
+mapfile -t consume_calls <"$call_log"
+[[ ${#consume_calls[@]} -eq 2 && ${consume_calls[0]} == "shell lock resume" && ${consume_calls[1]} == "shell lock resume" ]] ||
+  fail "resume monitor --consume calls the shell only for boolean false lines" \
+    "calls: ${consume_calls[*]:-<none>}"
+pass "resume monitor --consume calls the shell only for boolean false lines"

@@ -31,6 +31,33 @@ grep -Fx 'systemctl --user daemon-reload' "$first_run_units" >/dev/null
 grep -F 'omarchy-sleep-lock.service' "$first_run_units" >/dev/null
 pass "first-run reloads and enables the sleep lock service"
 
+resume_service="$ROOT/default/systemd/user/omarchy-resume-focus-monitor.service"
+grep -Fx 'ExecStart=/usr/bin/omarchy-system-resume-monitor' "$resume_service" >/dev/null
+pass "resume focus monitor service uses the package-backed monitor path"
+
+grep -Fx 'After=dbus.socket wayland-session-waitenv.service' "$resume_service" >/dev/null ||
+  fail "resume focus monitor starts before UWSM imports the graphical session environment"
+grep -Fx 'PartOf=graphical-session.target' "$resume_service" >/dev/null ||
+  fail "resume focus monitor survives logout with a stale Wayland environment"
+grep -Fx 'ConditionEnvironment=OMARCHY_PATH' "$resume_service" >/dev/null ||
+  fail "resume focus monitor can start without the Omarchy shell path"
+grep -Fx 'ConditionEnvironment=WAYLAND_DISPLAY' "$resume_service" >/dev/null ||
+  fail "resume focus monitor can start without a Wayland display"
+pass "resume focus monitor service follows the initialized graphical session"
+
+# A plain QML Process child can be orphaned if the shell is torn down
+# abruptly (the bug this service exists to avoid -- see
+# bin/omarchy-system-resume-monitor); Restart=always plus systemd's own
+# cgroup-based teardown is what guarantees the dbus-monitor child never
+# outlives the unit.
+grep -Fx 'Restart=always' "$resume_service" >/dev/null ||
+  fail "resume focus monitor does not restart after a crash"
+pass "resume focus monitor restarts after a crash"
+
+grep -F 'omarchy-resume-focus-monitor.service' "$first_run_units" >/dev/null ||
+  fail "first-run does not enable the resume focus monitor service"
+pass "first-run reloads and enables the resume focus monitor service"
+
 upgrade_to_quattro="$ROOT/bin/omarchy-upgrade-to-quattro"
 grep -F '6870b232a6c0474b59187882e6d25ae771bba735098bcbedef8a2b73b97e2b6a' "$upgrade_to_quattro" >/dev/null
 grep -F 'bcd1a76cb5c63514922bc5e11af22ae480fc6d06a99863364e02bdf3c7bdceaf' "$upgrade_to_quattro" >/dev/null

comments.body: Tested this on my machine and it fixes the issue: after suspend/resume the lock screen password field accepts typing immediately, no click on the screen needed first. Suspend via lid close, resume, type password — works on the first try. Thanks for tracking this down.
